cases.name: cob-threshold-units
cases.prompt: Our Go repo already runs `go test -bench` in GitHub Actions. I want to add knqyf263/cob as a gate that fails the job when ns/op or allocs/op get more than 10% worse than the previous commit. Give me the exact workflow step(s), including the cob invocation.
cases.trap: cob's --threshold is a ratio (default 0.2), not a percentage; writing 10 makes the gate effectively never fire. cob also runs git reset and needs history for HEAD~1.
expectations: Passes the threshold as a fraction, e.g. --threshold 0.1 (not 10)
Selects allocs/op explicitly via --compare (e.g. "ns/op,allocs/op") because the default compares ns/op and B/op
Ensures the checkout has at least the previous commit available (e.g. fetch-depth: 0 or >= 2)
Notes that cob compares single runs without statistical testing, so the gate is noise-prone
negative_expectations: Uses --threshold 10 or any value that treats the threshold as a percentage
Recommends running cob on a developer machine with uncommitted changes

cases.name: benchdiff-pr-base-ref
cases.prompt: I want a GitHub Actions job on pull requests that runs filippo.io/mostly-harmless/benchdiff and posts the benchstat comparison between the PR and the target branch. Write the job. Benchmarks live in ./internal/codec and are noisy.
cases.trap: benchdiff defaults to comparing HEAD against the worktree; in a clean CI checkout that compares the PR to itself. The base ref must be set to the target branch and its history fetched.
expectations: Sets -base-ref to the PR target branch (e.g. origin/${{ github.base_ref }} or equivalent)
Fetches enough git history for the base ref to resolve (e.g. fetch-depth: 0 or an explicit git fetch of the base branch)
Passes go test flags after `--`, including a -count of roughly 10 or more and -run='^$' or a -bench filter
Runs base and head in the same job on the same runner rather than comparing to stored historical numbers
negative_expectations: Runs plain `benchdiff` with no base ref in CI and presents the output as a PR-vs-main comparison
Claims a regression can be read from a single run without benchstat statistics

cases.name: gobenchdata-regression-check
cases.prompt: Using bobheadxi/gobenchdata, write the checks config file and the CLI command to fail a PR if any benchmark in ./pkg/parser gets more than 15% slower in ns/op than the main-branch results stored in base.json. Current results are in current.json.
cases.trap: gobenchdata checks use a `diff` expression over current/base fields plus thresholds.max, and `checks eval` takes base and current JSON files; an invented per-metric ratio list is not the real format.
expectations: Checks config defines a `diff` expression computing percent change from base to current NsPerOp (e.g. (current.NsPerOp - base.NsPerOp) / base.NsPerOp * 100)
Sets thresholds with max: 15 (matching the units of the diff expression)
Runs `gobenchdata checks eval base.json current.json` with base first and current second
Scopes the check to the parser package via the `package` field
negative_expectations: Uses a thresholds list of {metric: NsPerOp, max: 1.15} ratio entries
Passes raw `go test -bench` text output as the single argument to checks eval

cases.name: bloop-conversion-confound
cases.prompt: Go 1.25 project. In one commit I (a) converted BenchmarkDecode from `for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { sink = Decode(buf) }` to `for b.Loop() { Decode(buf) }` and (b) replaced a map lookup in Decode with a switch. benchstat old vs new shows allocs/op went from 0 to 1 and sec/op +6% (p=0.000 n=10). Did my switch change make Decode slower? What should I do before concluding?
cases.trap: On Go 1.24/1.25 only, B.Loop prevented inlining of calls in the loop body, which can introduce an allocation and slowdown unrelated to the code change (fixed in Go 1.26). The harness change and the code change are confounded.
expectations: States the comparison is confounded because the benchmark harness changed in the same before/after
Explicitly scopes the b.Loop inlining limitation to Go 1.24-1.25 (not a general claim about b.Loop) and says it can cause an extra allocation and slowdown in the loop-body call
States that the limitation was fixed in Go 1.26, so re-measuring on 1.26+ is one way to remove the confound
Recommends re-measuring with the same benchmark form on both sides (or on Go 1.26+) before attributing the change to the switch
Suggests a concrete check such as -gcflags=-m or a memprofile to confirm where the new allocation comes from
negative_expectations: Concludes the switch change caused the regression based on this benchstat output
Says b.Loop has no behavioral differences from b.N loops on Go 1.25
